questions.stem: A 58 year old man with a kidney transplant takes tacrolimus and prednisolone. He has a 10 day history of worsening headache, low-grade fever and right arm weakness. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. A contrast CT head shows a solitary left parietal lesion with a smooth enhancing rim and surrounding oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Immunosuppression (including steroids) is a risk factor; a subacute fever, headache and focal deficit with a solitary ring-enhancing lesion is a brain abscess.

steps.x: Immunosuppressed, febrile, subacute focal signs and a ring-enhancing lesion.

elim: Sudden onset, no fever, and does not ring-enhance.
Extra-axial, enhances uniformly and does not cause fever.
Usually enhances homogeneously and does not explain the fever.
A crescentic extra-axial collection, not a ring-enhancing lesion.

steps.x: A: Brain abscess. Fever + focal signs + solitary ring-enhancing lesion = brain abscess.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman had a craniotomy to remove a meningioma 3 weeks ago. She now has 5 days of headache and fever, and this morning had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Her wound is red with a small amount of discharge. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recent neurosurgery is a recognised source; fever, headache and a seizure with an infected wound suggest a postoperative brain abscess.

clues: red with a small amount of discharge
steps.x: Recent neurosurgery, infected wound, fever and a new seizure.

elim: Possible after surgery, but focal seizures with wound infection and a subacute course point to a parenchymal collection.
Does not explain the fever and wound discharge.
Does not cause fever or an infected wound.
Would not recur in 3 weeks or cause fever.

steps.x: B: Brain abscess. Neurosurgery or penetrating trauma is a route for brain abscess; seizures are a feature.

questions.stem: A 25 year old builder had a nail-gun injury that penetrated his left forehead 2 weeks ago. He has had a week of worsening headache, vomiting and fever, and now has weakness of his right arm and leg. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Penetrating trauma seeds infection; a subacute fever, raised ICP signs and contralateral weakness point to brain abscess.

clues: weakness of his right arm and leg
steps.x: Penetrating injury, fever, raised ICP and a contralateral focal deficit.

elim: Presents within hours of injury with a lucid interval, not fever after 2 weeks.
Would not appear within 2 weeks of a penetrating injury with fever.
Does not cause fever, papilloedema or persistent hemiparesis.
Does not cause fever, focal signs or papilloedema.

steps.x: A: Brain abscess. Head trauma is a source; abscess presents like a space-occupying lesion with fever.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a contrast CT head that shows a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontoparietal region with surrounding oedema. She had 2 weeks of maxillary sinusitis before developing headache and fever. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
questions.e: Mass effect and oedema cause deficits matching the lesion site; a left-sided motor cortex lesion causes right-sided weakness.

steps.x: Left hemisphere lesion with oedema.

elim: Suggests spinal cord or parasagittal pathology, not a unilateral lesion.
A left hemisphere lesion causes contralateral (right) weakness.
Horner syndrome; not caused by a frontoparietal lesion.
Cerebellar signs come from the posterior fossa, not the frontoparietal lobe.

steps.x: E: Right-sided hemiparesis. Hemiparesis is contralateral to the abscess.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man with a known right temporal brain abscess becomes drowsy on the ward. His GCS falls from 15 to 11. His right pupil is dilated and slow to react, his right eyelid droops and the right eye is deviated down and out. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 172/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
questions.e: Raised ICP from an expanding temporal abscess compresses the oculomotor nerve: ptosis, a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye.

steps.x: Raised ICP signs (falling GCS, bradycardia, hypertension) with a third nerve palsy.

elim: Causes failure of abduction with a normal pupil and eyelid.
Causes facial weakness, not ptosis with a dilated pupil.
Causes visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect, not ptosis or a down-and-out eye.
Causes vertical diplopia without ptosis or pupil change.

steps.x: C: Oculomotor nerve. Oculomotor palsy is a recognised sign of brain abscess with raised ICP: urgent escalation.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman is admitted with a 2 cm left frontal brain abscess and started on IV antibiotics. Two days later she has worsening headache, repeated vomiting and is drowsy, with a GCS of 12. Fundoscopy shows new bilateral papilloedema. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 58 bpm, BP 168/94 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L and sodium 138 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
questions.e: Headache, vomiting, drowsiness, papilloedema and a Cushing response (bradycardia, hypertension) show raised ICP from the abscess and its oedema.

steps.x: Raised ICP features with normal glucose and sodium.

elim: Rare, and does not cause papilloedema with bradycardia and hypertension.
Her glucose is normal.
Her sodium is normal.
Can cause drowsiness but not new papilloedema, bradycardia and hypertension.

steps.x: E: Raised intracranial pressure. Brain abscess causes symptoms via mass effect, oedema and raised ICP: vomiting, papilloedema, reduced GCS.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 12 day history of steadily worsening headache, night sweats and low-grade fever. For 3 days she has had weakness of her left hand. She had a root canal procedure a month ago. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A subacute headache with fever, raised inflammatory markers and a new focal deficit after dental work is a brain abscess.

clues: 12 day history of steadily worsening headache
steps.x: Subacute course, fever, focal signs, raised CRP, dental source.

elim: Does not usually cause fever or raised inflammatory markers.
Sudden onset; does not cause a 12 day headache with fever.
Recurrent and reversible, without fever or raised CRP.
A sudden thunderclap headache, not a subacute course.

steps.x: A: Brain abscess. Onset is typically subacute and inflammatory markers may be raised.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 week history of headache, fever and confusion. He has had chronic otitis media with a foul-smelling right ear discharge for months. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. He has mild left-sided weakness. A contrast-enhanced CT head is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Crescentic hyperdense collection over the convexity
Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
Multiple enhancing lesions at the grey–white junction
Solitary ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema
Wedge-shaped hypodensity in an arterial territory
questions.e: The best imaging clue for brain abscess is a solitary ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema and mass effect, here in the right temporal lobe from ear infection.

steps.x: Ear source, fever, subacute focal signs.

elim: This is an acute subdural haematoma.
This is subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Typical of metastases.
This is an ischaemic infarct.

steps.x: D: Solitary ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema. Solitary ring-enhancing lesion + oedema + mass effect = brain abscess.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe after a month of frontal sinusitis. Neurosurgeons aspirate thick pus. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains. The organism grows best in an atmosphere with added carbon dioxide and produces a caramel smell on culture.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive cocci in chains from a sinus-related frontal abscess is the Streptococcus milleri (anginosus) group, the classic brain abscess organism.

steps.x: Sinus source, chains of Gram-positive cocci.

elim: A Gram-negative rod; causes neonatal meningitis.
A Gram-positive rod; causes meningitis in the elderly and immunocompromised.
Gram-negative diplococci; causes meningitis, not abscess after sinusitis.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters; typical after trauma or neurosurgery.

steps.x: E: Streptococcus milleri group. Strep milleri is the classic brain abscess organism; Staph aureus after trauma or surgery.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has a 2 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right parietal lobe. He has no ear, sinus or dental symptoms. He has a 3 week history of fevers and weight loss. He has a pansystolic murmur at the apex and splinter haemorrhages. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the brain lesion?
questions.e: A new murmur, splinter haemorrhages and fevers point to endocarditis seeding the brain through the blood; blood cultures and echo look for it.

clues: no ear, sinus or dental symptoms
steps.x: No local source, but signs of endocarditis.

elim: He has no ear symptoms, and it causes temporal or cerebellar abscesses.
He has no dental symptoms.
He has no sinus symptoms, and it causes frontal lobe abscesses.
Can cause tuberculomas, but the murmur and splinter haemorrhages point to the heart.

steps.x: D: Infective endocarditis. Endocarditis is a key haematogenous source of brain abscess.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has her first generalised seizure. Her partner says she has had 2 weeks of headache and has seemed slow and confused for 3 days. A month ago she had a painful right ear with discharge after swimming, followed by tenderness behind the ear. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Otitis media then mastoiditis, followed by subacute headache, confusion, fever and a seizure, is a brain abscess from contiguous spread.

steps.x: Ear infection, mastoiditis, subacute headache and altered mental status, then a seizure.

elim: Nothing suggests alcohol excess, and it does not cause fever with a subacute headache.
Acute onset over days without a preceding ear and mastoid infection.
Does not cause fever, headache and confusion for weeks.
Self-limiting; does not usually cause seizures and confusion after mastoiditis.

steps.x: B: Brain abscess. A history of ear or sinus infection plus seizures and fever: think brain abscess.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has a 9 day history of headache and fever after a bout of mastoiditis. He has a mild left hemiparesis. A junior doctor plans a lumbar puncture to look for meningitis. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to perform first?
questions.e: Focal signs with fever after mastoiditis suggest a space-occupying abscess; image first with contrast CT (or urgent MRI) before any lumbar puncture.

steps.x: Focal deficit: imaging before LP.

elim: Not useful in suspected intracranial infection.
For seizures or encephalitis; it does not show a mass.
Dangerous with a possible space-occupying lesion; risks herniation.
Cannot show intracranial collections.

steps.x: B: Contrast-enhanced CT head. First-line: contrast-enhanced CT head or urgent MRI; LP is contraindicated with a mass lesion.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe on contrast CT. She has a 2 week history of headache and is afebrile. Her CRP is mildly raised. The team cannot tell whether this is an abscess or a necrotic tumour.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: MRI head is the urgent alternative to CT; on diffusion-weighted imaging pus restricts diffusion, which separates an abscess from a necrotic tumour.

steps.x: Ring lesion of uncertain cause.

elim: Does not characterise a mass.
Unsafe with a mass lesion and does not characterise it.
Not the next step; MRI characterises the lesion first.
Gives less information than the contrast CT already done.

steps.x: C: MRI head with diffusion-weighted imaging. Urgent MRI head characterises a ring-enhancing lesion; abscess shows restricted diffusion.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a 3 cm ring-enhancing right parietal lesion and has been started on IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Two sets of blood cultures taken before antibiotics are negative. The team wants to identify the organism to target treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Stereotactic aspiration of the lesion for culture
questions.e: Definitive microbiological diagnosis needs aspiration or drainage of the pus for Gram stain and culture, guiding targeted antibiotics.

steps.x: Imaging done, blood cultures negative, organism unknown.

elim: Unsafe with a mass lesion, and CSF is often sterile in abscess.
Confirms the lesion but does not identify the organism.
Already negative; aspiration is the definitive test.
Marks bacterial infection but does not identify the organism.

steps.x: E: Stereotactic aspiration of the lesion for culture. Gold standard: neuroimaging plus microbiology from aspiration or drainage.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man who injects drugs has a 1 week history of headache and fever. A contrast CT head shows a 2 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe. He has no ear, sinus or dental symptoms. The team is about to give the first dose of IV antibiotics.
questions.q: Which investigation should be taken before the first dose?
questions.e: Blood cultures (with inflammatory markers) look for a haematogenous source such as endocarditis, and must be taken before antibiotics.

clues: no ear, sinus or dental symptoms
steps.x: No local source; likely haematogenous.

elim: Does not identify the organism or an endocardial source.
Contraindicated with a space-occupying lesion.
Useful in sepsis, but it does not identify the organism.
The urinary tract is not a source of brain abscess.

steps.x: A: Blood cultures. Blood cultures and inflammatory markers look for the source, e.g. endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a left parietal brain abscess. Three sets of blood cultures grow viridans streptococci. She has a soft early diastolic murmur and a history of rheumatic fever. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 116/62 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the source?
questions.e: Positive blood cultures and a murmur suggest endocarditis as the haematogenous source; echocardiography looks for vegetations.

steps.x: Bacteraemia, murmur, damaged valve.

elim: She has no sinus symptoms, and the bloodstream infection points to the heart.
Viridans streptococci with a murmur point to the valves.
Contraindicated with a space-occupying lesion.
No back pain or cord signs.

steps.x: C: Echocardiogram. Blood cultures find the source, e.g. endocarditis; echo confirms it.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with poorly controlled diabetes has 2 weeks of headache, fever and new left-sided weakness. A dental abscess was drained a month ago. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. His CRP is 71 mg/L. The team discusses which approach will confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the gold-standard approach to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Brain abscess is confirmed by neuroimaging plus a microbiological diagnosis from aspiration or drainage; bloods and cultures only support it.

clues: 2 weeks of headache, fever and new left-sided weakness
steps.x: Likely abscess from a dental source; the question is what confirms it.

elim: Look for a source but are often negative and do not confirm the lesion.
Shows a ring-enhancing lesion but cannot prove it is pus or name the organism.
Unsafe with a mass lesion and often unhelpful.
Inflammatory markers are non-specific and may be normal.

steps.x: D: Neuroimaging with aspiration for microbiology. Gold standard = imaging + aspirate for microbiology.

questions.stem: A 43 year old man has a 3 cm left temporal brain abscess after chronic otitis media. Neurosurgery plans aspiration this afternoon. The registrar starts IV ceftriaxone and asks which drug to add to cover anaerobic organisms from the ear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to add?
questions.e: Empirical treatment is IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) plus metronidazole for anaerobes.

steps.x: Ear source, ceftriaxone already given, anaerobes uncovered.

elim: An antiviral for herpes encephalitis, not bacterial abscess.
Adds little to ceftriaxone and does not reliably cover anaerobes.
Penetrates the brain poorly and does not cover anaerobes.
Covers MRSA, not anaerobes.

steps.x: D: Metronidazole. Brain abscess: IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has had 48 hours of IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole for a right frontal brain abscess. Her headache is worse. Repeat contrast CT shows the abscess has grown from 2.5 cm to 3.5 cm with more oedema and mass effect. Her GCS is 14. Her temperature is 38.2°C and BP 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop antibiotics and repeat imaging in 2 weeks
questions.e: First-line treatment combines surgical drainage with IV antibiotics; an enlarging abscess with mass effect needs urgent neurosurgical drainage.

clues: has grown from 2.5 cm to 3.5 cm
steps.x: An enlarging abscess with mass effect despite antibiotics.

elim: Changing antibiotics does not replace drainage of an enlarging collection.
Contraindicated with mass effect.
She is getting worse; antibiotics must continue.
IV antibiotics are needed, and she needs drainage.

steps.x: E: Urgent neurosurgical aspiration or drainage. Drainage plus IV antibiotics; urgent neurosurgical review.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man is on the medical ward with a 3 cm left parietal brain abscess, awaiting transfer to neurosurgery. Overnight his GCS falls from 15 to 10 and he vomits twice. His pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 176/96 mmHg. His pupils are equal and reactive.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral antiemetic and review in the morning
questions.e: A falling GCS with bradycardia and hypertension shows raised ICP; escalate urgently for neurosurgical drainage and ICP management.

steps.x: Rapid neurological deterioration with a Cushing response.

elim: Too slow for a falling GCS; he needs urgent escalation.
Dangerous with raised ICP from a mass lesion.
Vomiting here is a sign of raised ICP, not a symptom to treat alone.
Irrelevant to his acute deterioration.

steps.x: E: Urgent escalation and neurosurgical review. Deterioration on neuro-observations = urgent escalation and neurosurgical review.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is admitted with a 2 cm right temporal brain abscess. She has started IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole and is awaiting aspiration tomorrow. She is alert with a GCS of 15. The nurse asks how she should be monitored overnight.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring?
o: Regular neurological observations including GCS and pupils
questions.e: Neurological observations (GCS, pupils, vital signs) pick up raised ICP early so deterioration can be escalated urgently.

steps.x: A stable abscess awaiting drainage that could deteriorate.

elim: Only for suspected non-convulsive seizures.
Contraindicated with a mass lesion.
Too infrequent to detect raised ICP early.
Imaging is repeated if she deteriorates, not routinely.

steps.x: D: Regular neurological observations including GCS and pupils. Neuro-observations with urgent escalation on deterioration.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man sees his GP with a 10 day history of worsening headache and fever after a frontal sinus infection. Today his wife noticed he was slurring his words and his right hand is clumsy. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 48 hours
Two-week wait referral for suspected brain tumour
questions.e: Fever, headache and new focal signs after sinusitis suggest a brain abscess: send to hospital as an emergency for imaging and neurosurgical review.

steps.x: Possible intracranial infection with focal signs.

elim: A new focal deficit with fever needs same-day imaging and specialist care.
Too slow; this may be a brain abscess.
Weeks of delay could be fatal.
Fever after sinusitis makes infection likely and needs emergency assessment.

steps.x: A: Emergency hospital admission. Suspected neurological infection with focal signs = emergency admission (NICE).

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a 2.5 cm left frontal brain abscess and is on IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole. This morning he had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, which stopped on its own. He is now recovering, with a GCS of 14. Neurosurgery plans aspiration later today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Seizures from a brain abscess are managed with an antiepileptic drug such as levetiracetam alongside antibiotics and drainage.

steps.x: A self-terminating seizure in a patient with an abscess.

elim: An antiviral for herpes encephalitis; it does not prevent seizures.
The seizure has stopped; benzodiazepines are for ongoing seizures.
Contraindicated with a mass lesion.
Seizures from a brain abscess should be treated to prevent recurrence.

steps.x: C: Levetiracetam. Manage seizures if present: start an antiepileptic; benzodiazepines only for ongoing seizures.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman who injects heroin has tricuspid and mitral valve endocarditis. She develops headache and left arm weakness. A contrast MRI head shows two small ring-enhancing lesions in different lobes, at the grey–white matter junction. She has no ear, sinus or dental symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route by which infection reached her brain?
o: Direct spread from a contiguous infected focus
Retrograde spread along the olfactory nerve
questions.e: Septic emboli from endocarditis travel in the blood, often causing multiple lesions at the grey–white junction: haematogenous spread.

clues: two small ring-enhancing lesions in different lobes
no ear, sinus or dental symptoms
steps.x: Endocarditis, multiple lesions, no local source.

elim: Gives a single lesion next to the ear or sinus; she has no local source.
The brain has no conventional lymphatic route for abscess formation.
Describes Naegleria, not bacterial abscess from endocarditis.
Causes meningitis or ventriculitis, not parenchymal abscesses.

steps.x: B: Haematogenous spread. Endocarditis seeds the brain haematogenously; ear, sinus and dental infections spread directly.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has had a painful, discharging left ear for a month and now has swelling and tenderness behind the ear that pushes the pinna forward. He develops headache, fever and unsteadiness. Contrast CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion adjacent to the left petrous temporal bone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the infection reached the brain?
o: Direct spread from a contiguous focus
Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
questions.e: Otitis media with mastoiditis spreads directly through bone to the adjacent temporal lobe or cerebellum.

clues: swelling and tenderness behind the ear
adjacent to the left petrous temporal bone
steps.x: Mastoiditis with a lesion next to the infected bone.

elim: No murmur or bacteraemia, and the lesion sits next to the infected ear.
Haematogenous route; the lesion is next to the infected mastoid.
Describes herpes encephalitis, not a pus collection.
Causes meningitis, not a focal parenchymal abscess.

steps.x: A: Direct spread from a contiguous focus. Ear, sinus and dental infections spread directly to the adjacent brain.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man develops headache and fever 10 days after a dental abscess. A contrast CT head on day 3 of symptoms shows a poorly defined area of low attenuation in the left frontal lobe with patchy enhancement but no rim. A repeat CT 2 weeks later shows a well-defined ring-enhancing lesion.
questions.q: Which best explains the appearance on the first scan?
o: Mature abscess with a fibrous capsule
questions.e: An abscess evolves from early and late cerebritis (no defined capsule) to a mature abscess whose fibrous capsule enhances as a ring around the non-enhancing necrotic centre.

clues: poorly defined area of low attenuation
steps.x: First scan: no capsule. Second scan: ring.

elim: Would appear hyperdense, not as poorly defined low attenuation.
Does not evolve into a ring-enhancing lesion with fever.
Gives a well-defined ring; this is the second scan.
Does not change from patchy enhancement to a ring within 2 weeks with fever.

steps.x: A: Early cerebritis without a capsule. Cerebritis has no capsule; the mature capsule enhances as a ring around necrotic pus.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 2.5 cm right parietal brain abscess. MRI shows extensive surrounding white matter oedema with midline shift. She has a dense left hemiparesis that is far larger than the size of the abscess would suggest.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the extent of her deficit?
questions.e: Inflammation around the abscess leaks fluid (vasogenic oedema); with mass effect it raises ICP and causes deficits matching the location.

clues: far larger than the size of the abscess
steps.x: Small abscess, large oedema, large deficit.

elim: Follows subarachnoid haemorrhage, not abscess.
Follows arterial occlusion; abscess oedema is vasogenic.
Seen in multiple sclerosis, not around an abscess.
Not shown, and it is not the main cause of deficit.

steps.x: E: Mass effect with vasogenic oedema. Focal deficits come from mass effect plus vasogenic oedema, matching the abscess location.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia has a known large pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. Ten days after a dental extraction she develops headache, fever and right-sided weakness. Contrast CT head shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe. Her echocardiogram is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which her lung condition predisposed to this lesion?
o: Bacteria bypassing the pulmonary capillary filter
Direct spread from the pulmonary malformation
Hypoxic damage to the blood–brain barrier
Infected vegetation on a heart valve
questions.e: A right-to-left shunt (a pulmonary AVM, like cyanotic congenital heart disease) lets bacteria from the blood bypass the lung capillaries that normally trap septic emboli.

steps.x: A right-to-left shunt in the lung, then a bacteraemia from dental work.

elim: The lung is not adjacent to the brain.
Not the mechanism of septic embolism.
HHT does not impair immunity.
Her echocardiogram is normal.

steps.x: A: Bacteria bypassing the pulmonary capillary filter. Right-to-left shunts bypass the pulmonary filter, so septic emboli reach the brain.
